Azure Cloud-Native Platform Updates

Follow meaningful documentation updates across Microsoft's Azure cloud-native platform, spanning container orchestration and fleet management (AKS, AKS Automatic, Application Network, AKS Support, AKS Arc, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, and Kubernetes Fleet Manager), container registry (Azure Container Registry), application networking (Application Gateway for Containers), and Azure Linux. The tracker also summarizes the latest five AKS and Application Network releases.

It automatically scans for changes, then uses AI to summarize and highlight updates that are most likely to matter — such as new features, deprecations, and significant content revisions.

Minor edits (like typos, formatting tweaks, and other low-impact changes) are usually filtered out. Because the process is automated, some updates may be missed or summaries may not capture every nuance.

For complete accuracy, you can always follow the provided links to the original Microsoft documentation.

With this tracker, you can:

  • Quickly scan meaningful AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet documentation changes from the past 7 days
  • Stay up to date with the latest AKS and App Net release notes without digging through every doc page
  • Search and browse CVE security data across AKS releases and VHD node images, powered by the AKS Vulnerability Data API (Public Preview)

Get the Latest AKS Docs - Every Week, in Your Inbox

Release 2026-10-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-27

The release on 2026-10-25 introduces automatic upgrades for unsupported Kubernetes versions and updates to node pools.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will automatically upgrade unsupported clusters after a grace period.
  • Default OS SKU for node pools changes to Ubuntu 26.04 with Kubernetes 1.38.
🔑

Key Features

  • Kubernetes 1.37 is now generally available as Long-Term Support.
  • Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) enhancements include new CRDs and features.
💡

Good to Know

  • Review upgrade channels to prepare for automated upgrades.
  • Community support for Kubernetes 1.34 ends by November 2026.

Release Notes 2026-09-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-01

The 2026-09-25 release introduces significant updates and deprecations. Key features include the general availability of identity bindings and preview support for Ubuntu 26.04.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • Windows Server 2022 is not supported in Kubernetes version 1.37 and above.
  • Flatcar Container Linux node images are removed, affecting scaling operations.
  • The annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-pip-tags no longer overrides public IP tags.
🔑

Key Features

  • Identity bindings are now generally available.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 is available in preview.
  • Windows Server OS SKU migration to 2025 is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • AKS will auto-migrate deprecated Availability Sets clusters after September 30, 2026.
  • AKS release order has been updated for Central US and East US.
  • Check AKS Release Tracker for detailed release timing.

Release 2026-09-04

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-09-09

This release introduces Kubernetes 1.37 and autoscaling for VM node pools. It also announces the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will remove Azure Linux with OS Guard node images on March 10, 2027.
  • AKS no longer produces VHDs for Windows Server 2019 and version 23H2.
🔑

Key Features

  • Autoscaling for Virtual Machines node pools is now generally available.

💡

Good to Know

  • LocalDNS is enabled automatically for compatible cluster networking.
  • AKS rejects updates that remove IPv6 from dual-stack clusters.
  • Managed namespace creation rejects names starting with reserved prefixes.

Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026: - Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools. - AKS won’t produce new node images for affected node pools. - Existing node pools won’t receive security patches. On March 10, 2027, AKS will remove the Azure Linux with OS Guard node images. After the images are removed, scaling and remediation operations, including reimage and redeploy operations, will fail for affected node pools. You can use either of the following migration options: - Migrate an existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool in place by following the Migrate nodes to Azure Container Linux for Azure Kubernetes Service documentation. This operation preforms a standard node image upgrade. - Alternatively, create a new Azure Container Linux node pool, migrate and validate workloads, and then delete the Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool. Follow Add Azure Container Linux node pools and remove existing node pools. For other available options, see the AKS node operating system. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub Repository. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

Ubuntu 20.04 has been replaced by newer supported versions, including Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04. We encourage you to transition to Ubuntu 22.04+ before the retirement date. If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with Federal Information Process Standard (FIPS) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ where Ubuntu 22.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for FIPS workloads. On March 31, 2027 Azure Monitor will be deprecating the sidecar for remote-write of Prometheus metrics to Azure Monitor Workspace. This is as part of our ongoing efforts to improve reliability and reduce complexity. We recommend configuring your self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to remote-write directly to Azure Monitor Workspace. All authentication methods are supported in the Prometheus remote-write configuration, and direct remote-write is fully compatible with the Prometheus Operator. You can find detailed configuration guidance in the official documentation. This approach removes the need for the sidecar and simplifies your setup. We encourage you to transition to direct Prometheus remote-write as soon as possible to take advantage of the improved experience and ensure uninterrupted service. If you have any questions or need assistance during this transition, please feel free to contact ciprometheus@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription IDs.

Newer supported versions include kernel updates and security improvements. Until June 30, 2027, you can continue to use Ubuntu 22.04 on AKS without disruption. If you don't migrate by June 30, 2027, you won't be able to create new node pools, AKS won't produce new node images, and you'll no longer receive security patches for existing node pools. On April 30, 2028 AKS will remove Ubuntu 22.04 node images and existing code, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Migration Options: - Default Operating System SKU (OSSku): If you're using 'Ubuntu,' you'll automatically migrate to Ubuntu 24.04 when you upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.35 or later. - Versioned OSSku: If you're using 'Ubuntu2204,' update your OSSku to 'Ubuntu' for Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or 'Ubuntu2404' for Kubernetes 1.32 or later. Read moreRead less
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters: - Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase) - Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready) After this change: - Metric names remain unchanged. - Aggregate pod counts remain available. - Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported. - The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting. During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement. You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow: - Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension. - Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension. Recommended action: - If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required. - If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native pod metrics. Help and support If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027. Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster. After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support. Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

Azure Container Registry (ACR) implements Docker Content Trust (DCT), allowing image publishers to sign their images and image consumers to verify that the images they pull are signed. With advancements in technology, Docker Content Trust no longer meets the requirements of modern supply chain security for containers. As a result, Docker Content Trust will be deprecated and no longer available in ACR after March 31, 2028. If you currently use Docker Content Trust, you should transition to the Notary Project ecosystem, including their open-source supply chain tool, Notation. How does this affect me? - Starting September 30, 2025, customers will no longer be able to enable Docker Content Trust on Azure Container Registry. - Data stored in Azure Container Registry for signing and verifying signatures with Docker Content Trust will be permanently deleted on March 31, 2028. - Docker Content Trust function will be completely removed from Azure Container Registry on March 31, 2028. Required Action Start your transition to Notary Project today and enhance the security and trust of your container ecosystem. Use the following articles to get started. Signing: - Use AKV with self-signed certificates - Use AKV with CA-issued certificates - Sign in ADO pipelines - Sign in GitHub workflows Verification: - Verify in ADO pipelines - Verify in GitHub workflows - Verify on AKS

Read moreRead less
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS will be retired on November 30, 2025, please transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by that date. Azure Linux 2.0 has been replaced by the newer supported version Azure Linux 3.0. We encourage you to transition to Azure Linux 3.0 prior to the retirement date to experience the capabilities of Azure Linux 3.0 including kernel updates and security improvements. From now to November 30, 2025, you can continue to use Azure Linux 2.0 without disruption. On November 30, 2025, Azure Linux 2.0 will no longer be supported on AKS; AKS will no longer create new node pools, produce new node images, or provide security updates for Azure Linux 2.0 after that date. On March 31, 2026, Azure Linux 2.0 node images will be removed. This will cause scaling operations to fail. Customers can transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by taking one of the following actions: - If you’re currently using Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.32+. - Alternately, starting Kubernetes version 1.28+ you can perform an in-place node pool update from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3, enabling you to migrate existing node pools from Azure Linux 2.0 to 3.0 while remaining on the same k8s version. Your node pool will automatically reimage to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 node image. See documentation here. To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Linux 3.0 by November 30, 2025.

Each image includes the packages and dependencies needed to support a specific application or workload.++Golden containers provide a standardized foundation for running common applications and services, reducing the need to build and maintain custom container images.++The following golden container images are available:++- BusyBox+- NGINX+- Node.js+- PostgreSQL+- Python+- PyTorch+- Telegraf+ ## Azure Linux container image tagging policy -The Azure Linux team tags every base container image upload with the `base/core:MajorVersion` and `base/core:FullVersion` tags.+The Azure Linux team tags every base container image upload with the `core:MajorVersion` and `core:FullVersion` tags.  The format of the tags is as follows: -- `Major Version`: X.X, where X.X is the major version number of the release (Example: 4.0).-- `Full Version`: `MajorVersion`.YYYYMMDD, where YYYYMMDD is the date the image was built (Example: 4.0.20260602).+- `Major Version`: The major version number of the release (for example, `4` for Azure Linux 4).+- `Full Version`: `YYYYMMDDRR`, where `YYYYMMDD` is the date the image was built and `RR` is the revision for that day, usually `00`. -This results in a `base/core:MajorVersion` tag that always represents the latest base container image release for a given major release, and a growing list of `base/core:FullVersion` tags that preserve a tag for each base container image that was pushed. Once a new major version of Azure Linux is released, base container image updates for the prior release continue to be published until the prior release is end of life.+This results in a `core:MajorVersion` tag that always represents the latest base container image release for a given major release, and a growing list of `core:FullVersion` tags that preserve a tag for each base container image that was pushed.                                                                             @@ -1,67 +1,113 @@-# Install Debug Symbol Packages on Azure Linux | Microsoft Learn+# Install debug symbol packages on Azure Linux | Microsoft Learn -Debug symbol (`debuginfo`) RPMs contain the symbol tables that debuggers and profilers, such as `gdb`, use to resolve addresses to function names and source lines. It's not suitable for production use.+This article explains where Azure Linux 4 publishes `debuginfo` packages, how to enable the production `base` debug symbol repository, and how to install symbols that match your installed packages.  ## Prerequisites -- An Azure Linux system that you can authenticate to with shell access.-- A user account with `sudo` privileges, which is required to write `.repo` files under `/etc/yum.repos.d/` and to install packages.+- An Azure Linux system with shell access, DNF5, and the Azure Linux repository configuration.+- A user account with `sudo` privileges to change repository settings and install packages.+- Access to `packages.microsoft.com` to download repository metadata and packages.  ## Where Azure Linux publishes `debuginfo` packages -Azure Linux publishes `debuginfo` RPMs to [packages.microsoft.com](https://packages.microsoft.com/) (PMC) in a dedicated location, organized by release version, release stage, and architecture. For Azure Linux 4.0, the layout is:+Azure Linux publishes `debuginfo` RPMs to [packages.microsoft.com](https://packages.microsoft.com/) (PMC), organized by major release, package channel, repository, and architecture. For Azure Linux 4 distribution packages in `base`, the layout is:  ```text-https://packages.microsoft.com/azurelinux/4.0/<STAGE>/base/debuginfo/<ARCH>/+https://packages.microsoft.com/azurelinux/4/<STAGE>/base/debuginfo/<ARCH>/ ``` -- **`<STAGE>`** is `beta` for packages in Azure Linux preview.-- **`<ARCH>`** is the target architecture, such as `x86_64` or `aarch64`.+- `<STAGE>` is `prod` for production packages or `preview` for packages in the public testing channel. Use symbols from the channel that supplied the binary package. Don't enable preview repositories to obtain symbols for production packages.+- `<ARCH>` is the package architecture, such as `x86_64` or `aarch64`.++For example, production symbols for `base` packages on x86-64 systems are published at:++```text+https://packages.microsoft.com/azurelinux/<AZURE_LINUX_VERSION>/prod/base/debuginfo/x86_64/+``` -The version, stage, and architecture must match the system the symbols will be loaded on. Mismatched `debuginfo` packages don't resolve symbols correctly.+Azure Linux 4.0 and later 4.x image versions share the `azurelinux/4` namespace. Symbols must match the binary's exact build, including its package epoch, version, release, and architecture. Matching only the major Azure Linux release isn't sufficient.  ## Enable the `debuginfo` repository -1. Install the config-manager plugin using the following command:+On Azure Linux 4.0, `dnf` invokes DNF5. Use the following steps for packages from the production `base` repository.++1. Check that the repository is configured, even if it's disabled:++    ```bash+    dnf repo list --all+    dnf repo info --all azurelinux-base azurelinux-base-debuginfo+    ```++    Confirm that `azurelinux-base` points to `/azurelinux/4/prod/base/` and `azurelinux-base-debuginfo` points to `/azurelinux/4/prod/base/debuginfo/` for your architecture. If either repository is missing or points to another channel, stop and verify your image's repository configuration before continuing. Enabling a repository doesn't create a missing definition or change its base URL.+2. Install the config-manager plugin:      ```bash     sudo dnf install 'dnf5-command(config-manager)'     ```-2. To install `debuginfo` packages, configure DNF to read from the Azure Linux `debuginfo` repository for your release and architecture:+3. Enable the production `base` debug symbol repository:      ```bash     sudo dnf config-manager setopt azurelinux-base-debuginfo.enabled=1     ```-3. Confirm that the `debuginfo` repository is enabled using the following command:+4. Confirm that the production `base` and debug symbol repositories are enabled:      ```bash-    dnf repolist+    dnf repo info --all azurelinux-base azurelinux-base-debuginfo     ``` -    The output should list the new `debuginfo` repository alongside the default Azure Linux repositories.+    Check the enabled/disabled status in the output. Both `azurelinux-base` and `azurelinux-base-debuginfo` should be enabled.  ## Install a debug symbol package -After the `debuginfo` repository is enabled, install symbol packages with `dnf install`. Debug symbol packages share the binary package's name and add a `-debuginfo` suffix. For example, to install symbols for `glibc`, run:+Debug symbol package names commonly end in `-debuginfo`, such as `glibc-debuginfo` and `openssl-debuginfo`. A symbol package can cover multiple binary subpackages from the same source package, so don't assume that every installed package has a symbol package with the same name. -```bash-sudo dnf install glibc-debuginfo-```+The following example installs symbols for the installed `glibc` package. -To install symbols for several packages at once, list each `-debuginfo` package on the command line. For example:+1. Check the installed binary package: -```bash-sudo dnf install glibc-debuginfo openssl-debuginfo-```+    ```bash+    dnf info --installed glibc+    ``` -After installation, debuggers and profilers automatically pick up the new symbols from `/usr/lib/debug/`.+    Record its epoch, version, release, and architecture.+2. Refresh the debug symbol repository metadata and list all available versions, not just the latest: -Tip+    ```bash+    dnf --refresh --repo=azurelinux-base-debuginfo info --available --showduplicates glibc-debuginfo+    ```++    Find the symbol package that matches the installed binary's epoch, version, release, and architecture.++    The `debuginfo` package must match the installed binary package so that debugging tools, such as `crash` and `gdb`, can correctly map crash data to functions, variables, and source code.+3. Install that exact symbol package:++    ```bash+    sudo dnf --repo=azurelinux-base,azurelinux-base-debuginfo install 'glibc-debuginfo-<EPOCH>:<VERSION>-<RELEASE>.<ARCH>'+    ```++    Replace the placeholders with the matching values. If the package has no epoch, omit `<EPOCH>:`. The `--repo` option limits this transaction to the production `base` and `base` debug symbol repositories. Review the proposed transaction before confirming it.++    To install symbols for several packages, add each exact symbol package identifier to the command. Match each one to its corresponding binary package rather than assuming they share a version.+4. Confirm the installed symbol package:++    ```bash+    dnf info --installed glibc-debuginfo+    ```++Debug symbol packages install separate debug files under `/usr/lib/debug/`. GDB can load matching separate debug files automatically. Other debuggers and profilers might require their own symbol-path configuration.++Important++If the exact matching symbols aren't available, don't substitute symbols from another version, architecture, or channel. Verify the binary's source repository and the symbol package name. For a core dump or copied executable, match the symbols to the binary that produced it, not necessarily the package currently installed on your troubleshooting system.++## Disable the debug symbol repository++If you no longer need the repository enabled, disable it:++```bash+sudo dnf config-manager setopt azurelinux-base-debuginfo.enabled=0+``` -Match the `debuginfo` package version to the binary package version that's installed on the system. Mismatched versions cause the debugger to fall back to address-only stack traces. Run `dnf info <package>-debuginfo` to confirm the available version before you install.+Disabling the repository doesn't uninstall symbol packages that are already installed.

Unlike the standard `acr purge` flow, which requires `--filter` and `--ago`, this flag makes those parameters optional. Without `--filter`, it scans all repositories. You can combine it with `--ago` to filter by age and `--keep` to preserve a number of recent untagged manifests.+- `--untagged-only` - Deletes only untagged manifests (dangling manifests that have no tags) without deleting any tags first. This flag makes `--filter` and `--ago` optional, unless you specify `--min-untagged-manifests`, which requires `--ago`. Without `--filter`, it scans all repositories. You can combine it with `--ago` to filter by age and `--keep` to preserve a number of recent untagged manifests, or use minimum and maximum manifest retention counts instead of `--keep`. - `--include-locked` - Purges tags and manifests even when they're locked (that is, their `write-enabled` or `delete-enabled` attributes are set to `false`). For each matching locked artifact, `acr purge` first unlocks it by setting both attributes back to `true`, then deletes it. Without this flag, locked tags and manifests are skipped. Caution@@ -209,6 +213,42 @@ az acr run \   /dev/null ``` +### Example: Combine age and retention counts++The following example protects the newest 10 matching tags in `hello-world` and selects other matching tags for deletion if they're older than three days or outside the newest 50.++```azurecli+PURGE_CMD="acr purge \+  --filter 'hello-world:.*' --ago 3d \+  --min-tags 10 --max-tags 50"++az acr run \+  --cmd "$PURGE_CMD" \+  --registry myregistry \+  /dev/null+```++To apply a similar policy to untagged manifests without deleting tags, use `--untagged-only` with the manifest retention flags. This example protects the newest 20 untagged manifests and selects others if they're older than three days or outside the newest 100:++```azurecli+PURGE_CMD="acr purge \+  --filter 'hello-world:.*' --untagged-only --ago 3d \+  --min-untagged-manifests 20 --max-untagged-manifests 100"++az acr run \+  --cmd "$PURGE_CMD" \+  --registry myregistry \+  /dev/null+```++To apply both policies in one command, use `--untagged` instead of `--untagged-only` and specify both tag and manifest retention flags.++Note++Retention counts must be zero or greater, and a minimum can't exceed its corresponding maximum. A minimum of `0` protects nothing. A maximum of `0` selects all matching items. Minimum flags require `--ago`, even when set to `0`. Manifest retention flags require `--untagged` or `--untagged-only`. Tag retention flags can't be used with `--untagged-only`.++Locked items count toward retention limits but aren't deleted unless you specify `--include-locked`. Locks, dependencies on retained image indexes, or skipped deletions can prevent a maximum count from being satisfied.+ ## Purge in ABAC-enabled registries  Registries with Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) enabled use repository-scoped permissions instead of registry-wide roles. The `acr purge` command automatically detects ABAC-enabled registries and adjusts its authentication — no additional flags are needed.

                                                                                                              @@ -140,6 +140,41 @@ spec:   fipsMode: FIPS ``` +## Workload runtime and pod sandboxing++NAP supports [pod sandboxing](concepts-pod-sandboxing) on provisioned nodes. The `spec.workloadRuntime` field determines the workload runtimes available on nodes that use an `AKSNodeClass`.++| Value | Behavior |+| --- | --- |+| `OCIContainer` | Default when omitted. Runs standard OCI containers. |+| `KataVmIsolation` | Enables pod sandboxing with Kata Containers alongside standard OCI containers. Pods that specify `runtimeClassName: kata-vm-isolation` run in lightweight VMs with their own guest kernel. |++Setting `workloadRuntime: KataVmIsolation` doesn't sandbox every pod on the node. Pods that don't request the Kata runtime continue to run as standard containers and can share the same node.++### Pod sandboxing requirements++- Set `imageFamily: AzureLinux`. NAP requires Azure Linux 3 for pod sandboxing, which requires Kubernetes version 1.32 or later.+- Use AMD64, generation 2 VM sizes with compatible virtualization capabilities. Karpenter automatically filters for compatible sizes and selects the Kata-enabled Azure Linux image. If you constrain VM sizes in a `NodePool`, leave compatible sizes available.+- Don't set `fipsMode: FIPS` or enable Trusted Launch. Pod sandboxing doesn't support either configuration.++The following example enables pod sandboxing for nodes provisioned from the `AKSNodeClass`:++```yaml+apiVersion: karpenter.azure.com/v1beta1+kind: AKSNodeClass+metadata:+  name: kata+spec:+  imageFamily: AzureLinux+  workloadRuntime: KataVmIsolation+```++Reference this `AKSNodeClass` from a Karpenter `NodePool` through `spec.template.spec.nodeClassRef`. For a complete walkthrough, including node pool configuration and workload deployment, see [Use Pod sandboxing with node auto-provisioning](use-pod-sandboxing#enable-pod-sandboxing-on-an-existing-cluster).++Important++Changing `workloadRuntime` on an existing `AKSNodeClass` doesn't install the runtime on running nodes in place. NAP replaces drifted nodes subject to the referencing `NodePool` disruption controls. Review [Drift](node-auto-provisioning-disruption#drift) before changing an existing configuration.+ ## Instance-level public IP configuration  You can assign a public IPv4 address to each NAP-provisioned node by setting `nodePublicIP.enabled` to `true`. You can optionally specify `ipTags` or `prefixIDs`. Use one or the other, not both.

                                                                                                                @@ -15,6 +15,18 @@ This article provides an overview of the security features in Azure Kubernetes A  - Certificates are currently issued by an Azure Kubernetes Application Network-managed certificate authority (CA) and aren't chained to a public CA. +## Ztunnel pod security requirements++On each eligible Linux node, the managed `ztunnel` DaemonSet handles mesh traffic for enrolled pods. Its `istio-proxy` container in `applink-system` requires the following settings:++| Setting | Why ztunnel needs it |+| --- | --- |+| `runAsUser: 0`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: true` | The proxy runs as root and enters workload network namespaces. It doesn't request a fully privileged container (`privileged: false`). |+| Linux capabilities `NET_ADMIN`, `SYS_ADMIN`, and `NET_RAW` | The proxy drops all capabilities, then adds these three for transparent proxying, switching network namespaces, and socket operations. |+| `hostPath` mount at `/var/run/ztunnel` | The proxy uses a node-local socket to communicate with the Istio CNI agent. |++Before joining a cluster, review all admission policies that apply to `applink-system`, including Azure Policy assignments inherited from a management group and policies enforced by other admission controllers. An AKS Deployment Safeguards exclusion doesn't change those policies. If an exception is needed, have your policy owner scope it to the managed workload as narrowly as the policy allows. Keep application workloads out of `applink-system` and keep their protections in place.+ ## mTLS  Application Network uses mTLS to provide identity-based, encrypted communication between workloads. Each service in an Application Network connected cluster automatically receives a certificate that allows it to prove its identity and establish trusted, encrypted connections with other services in the same Application Network. Encryption in transit uses FIPS-compliant cryptography.

It describes common errors, their causes, and solutions that get your pending pods running.  When you deploy workloads in AKS, you might encounter scheduler errors that prevent pods from running. The following sections describe common errors, their causes, and how to resolve them. -## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y node(s) had volume node affinity conflict+## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes had volume node affinity conflict  Note @@ -15,7 +15,7 @@ X and Y represent the number of nodes. These values depend on your cluster confi Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error message.  >-> 0/(X) nodes are available: Y node(s) had volume node affinity conflict.+> 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes had volume node affinity conflict.  ### Cause @@ -82,6 +82,29 @@ Follow these steps to resolve the insufficient CPU issue: 3. Optimize pod resource requests. Ensure that CPU requests and limits are appropriate for your node sizes. 4. Check if any scheduling constraints are restricting pod placement across available nodes. +## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Insufficient memory++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y Insufficient memory.++### Cause++The pod's effective memory request exceeds the remaining allocatable request budget on eligible nodes.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the insufficient memory issue:++1. Inspect the admitted memory requests and node accounting.++    ```bash+    kubectl describe pod <pod-name>+    kubectl describe node <eligible-node>+    ```+2. Right-size requests based on the application's needs, free legitimately reserved capacity, or provide an eligible node large enough for the pod.+ ## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y node(s) had untolerated taint  Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following error message.@@ -126,12 +149,292 @@ Follow these steps to resolve the untolerated taint issue:     kubectl get pods -o wide     ``` +## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Insufficient ephemeral-storage++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y Insufficient ephemeral-storage.++### Cause++The pod requests more local ephemeral storage than eligible nodes can allocate after other requests. This resource is separate from a PVC or Azure Disk's requested size.++This scheduler rejection differs from a pod that was scheduled and later evicted because of local-storage pressure. Memory-backed `emptyDir` volumes consume memory rather than this local-storage budget.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the insufficient ephemeral-storage issue:++1. Inspect requests, node allocatable storage, and allocated resources:++    ```bash+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl describe node <eligible-node>+    ```+2. Correct erroneous units or an unrealistic request. Size the request for the workload's writable layer, disk-backed `emptyDir`, logs, and other applicable local storage.+3. If the request is legitimate, provide suitable eligible node storage or capacity. Increasing a PVC's size doesn't increase node ephemeral storage.+4. If events instead show eviction or `DiskPressure`, investigate consumption and the node condition rather than treating it as this request-fit error.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu.++### Cause++Eligible nodes can't satisfy the pod's advertised `nvidia.com/gpu` request. Possible conditions include:++- No suitable GPU node is available.+- GPU requests from other pods reserve the exposed devices.+- A GPU VM exists, but the supported driver or device-plugin configuration isn't healthy or doesn't expose the expected resource.+- Taints, selectors, or affinity exclude otherwise usable GPU nodes.++A mixed rejection message doesn't establish which of these conditions caused a specific report.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the insufficient GPU issue:++1. Inspect the live GPU request and node resource advertisement:++    ```bash+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl describe node <gpu-node>+    kubectl get daemonsets,pods -n kube-system -o wide+    ```+2. Distinguish absent allocatable GPU resources from resources already reserved by requests. A GPU VM size or low observed GPU utilization alone isn't sufficient.+3. Verify the GPU pool's supported configuration and driver/device-plugin health. Follow [managed AKS GPU guidance](/en-us/azure/aks/aks-managed-gpu-nodes); don't install a second device plugin indiscriminately into a managed configuration.+4. For genuine capacity shortage, make an eligible GPU node available and inspect scale-up events, SKU restrictions, quota, and allocation failures. The [official AKS/KEDA example](/en-us/azure/aks/autoscale-gpu-workloads-with-keda) documents this scheduling error as a capacity signal.+5. Correct compatible placement/tolerations where necessary. Don't send an application to system nodes merely to bypass `CriticalAddonsOnly`.+6. Verify both scheduling and GPU functionality. Removing the GPU request isn't a validated remedy for a GPU-dependent application.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Node selector, affinity, or anti-affinity rules++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with one of the following scheduler errors.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't match Pod's node affinity or selector.+>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't match pod affinity rules.+>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't match pod anti-affinity rules.+>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't satisfy existing pods anti-affinity rules.++### Cause++A required placement rule excludes the candidate nodes. The rule can apply to node labels or to the location of other pods:++- **Node selector/node affinity:** Node labels don't satisfy the pod's `nodeSelector` or required node affinity. If you configure both, the node labels must satisfy both. All selector labels must match. Required affinity terms are alternatives, while expressions within a term must all match.+- **Pod affinity:** No matching pod is found in the required namespace and topology domain.+- **Pod anti-affinity:** The incoming pod excludes domains occupied by matching pods, or an existing pod's rule excludes the incoming pod from its domain. An existing pod's rule can reject the incoming pod even if the incoming pod has no anti-affinity.++Preferred affinity rules alone don't cause these hard rejections. For self-affinity, a pod that matches its own selector can schedule without an peer when the other first-pod exception conditions are met.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the placement rule mismatch:++1. Inspect the live pod's selectors and affinity rules, and compare them with node labels:++    ```bash+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get nodes --show-labels+    ```+2. For pod affinity or anti-affinity, inspect pods in the relevant namespaces and topology domains. Check label selectors, namespace scope, and `topologyKey`. For anti-affinity, also inspect existing pods' rules:++    ```bash+    kubectl get pods -A -o wide+    kubectl get pod <existing-pod-name> -n <existing-pod-namespace> -o yaml+    ```+3. Apply the fix for the affected rule:++    **Node selector/node affinity:** Correct mistaken or stale selector or label values, or provide nodes that meet the requirement.++    **Pod affinity:** Restore the intended matching pod or correct the selector, namespace, or topology key. The matching pod must be in a domain the incoming pod can also use.++    **Pod anti-affinity:** Make another genuine topology domain eligible by adding suitable nodes or correcting an overly restrictive node selector. Keep all applicable required anti-affinity exclusions satisfied.+4. Make workload changes through the controller's pod template. Correct unintended rules or label matches, and relax required rules only when hardware, security, and availability requirements permit it. Don't falsify hardware or topology labels, delete unrelated production peers as a routine fix, or use `spec.nodeName` to bypass scheduling.+5. Confirm the pending or replacement pod schedules on an eligible node in a permitted topology domain. Recheck current events and verify that both incoming and existing pods' required policies are satisfied.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't match pod topology spread constraints++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't match pod topology spread constraints.++### Cause++A hard spread constraint (`whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`) can't place the pod without exceeding `maxSkew`. Eligible domains depend on topology labels, selectors or affinity, and the configured node inclusion policies.++When there are fewer eligible domains than `minDomains`, the global minimum becomes zero. A cluster can have several nodes but only one eligible domain for a particular pod.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the topology spread constraint issue:++1. Inspect the constraint, selected replicas, and node labels:++    ```bash+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l <spread-selector> -o wide+    kubectl get nodes --show-labels+    ```++    - Check `topologyKey`, `labelSelector`, `maxSkew`, `minDomains`, `nodeAffinityPolicy`, and `nodeTaintsPolicy`. Restore sufficient genuinely eligible domains or correct an unintended restriction.+2. Change skew or domain requirements only after assessing availability intent. `ScheduleAnyway` makes the policy soft; successful placement after that change doesn't prove the original hard requirement is met.+3. Verify the resulting distribution.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y Too many pods++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y Too many pods.++### Cause++Eligible nodes reached the scheduler's pod-count limit. Available CPU or memory doesn't override node allocatable `pods` or node pool `maxPods`.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the pod-count limit issue:++1. Check the limit and assigned pods.++    ```bash+    kubectl describe node <eligible-node>+    kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=<eligible-node> -o wide+    ```+2. Account for system DaemonSets and other workloads, not only the application's replicas.+3. Release capacity by removing only legitimately obsolete workloads, or add eligible nodes. If changing `maxPods` requires a new pool, plan that change with the supported AKS networking/IP limits.+4. Confirm the pending pod schedules after a slot becomes available. Don't patch node capacity to fabricate slots.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes were unschedulable++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes were unschedulable.++### Cause++All eligible nodes are cordoned (`spec.unschedulable: true`) or otherwise excluded by the corresponding scheduling condition. This condition can be intentional during maintenance.++A condition-related untolerated-taint message can also mention `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable`.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the unschedulable node issue:++1. Inspect the node and maintenance context.++    ```bash+    kubectl get node <node-name> -o yaml+    kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>+    ```+2. If maintenance is complete and the node is safe to use, uncordon that specific node.++    ```bash+    kubectl uncordon <node-name>+    ```+3. Otherwise, provide another eligible node or wait for authorized maintenance to complete. Don't globally uncordon nodes or add a blanket toleration to bypass maintenance.+4. Confirm node state and pod scheduling.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.++### Cause++A claim that must bind before scheduling is still unbound. Possible causes include an incorrect or unavailable provisioner, provisioning or authorization failures, missing storage capacity, incompatible volume matching, or storage topology.++A pending `WaitForFirstConsumer` claim alone isn't this error.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaim issue:++1. Inspect the claim's events and class.++    ```bash+    kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n <namespace>+    kubectl get pvc <pvc-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get storageclass <storageclass-name> -o yaml+    ```+2. Verify the provisioner is available and inspect its controllers and events. Resolve the actual authorization, SKU, capacity, or binding error rather than scaling CPU nodes blindly.+3. For new topology-aware Azure Disk claims, choose an appropriate working class by using `WaitForFirstConsumer`.+4. Preserve existing data and reclaim-policy semantics. Before replacing an unbound claim, verify that it has no data to preserve and that replacement is appropriate. Don't delete production claims as a generic binding remedy.+5. Confirm binding, pod scheduling, successful mounting, and a real data-access check.++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes exceed max volume count++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes exceed max volume count.++### Cause++The pod's distinct CSI volumes, together with volumes already needed on the node, exceed the driver's advertised per-node attachment count. This condition isn't a disk-size limit or a CPU shortage.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the maximum volume count issue:++1. Inspect the real driver limit and claims:++    ```bash+    kubectl get csinode <eligible-node> -o yaml+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get pvc -n <namespace>+    ```+2. For Azure Disks, examine `disk.csi.azure.com` under `CSINode.spec.drivers`, including `allocatable.count`. Compare volume demand from this and other assigned pods.+3. Place the workload on an eligible node size with sufficient real attachment capacity, distribute workloads appropriately, or use a storage design suitable for the required volume count.+4. Keep storage topology and access modes compatible. Fewer GiB per disk don't reduce the number of attachments.+5. Confirm every required volume mounts and supports real data access. Don't patch CSI limits or fabricate volume handles. See [Azure Disk per-node volume guidance](/en-us/azure/aks/azure-disks-dynamic-pv).++## Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports++Pods remain in the **Pending** state with the following scheduler error.++>+> Error: 0/(X) nodes are available: Y nodes didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports.++### Cause++Another assigned pod reserves an overlapping `hostPort` on eligible nodes. The scheduler checks requested host IP, protocol, and port; a CPU-capacity increase on the same node doesn't release that reservation.++This error isn't a Service `NodePort` allocation error. A host process causing a bind failure after placement is also a different diagnostic path.++### Solution++Follow these steps to resolve the unavailable host-port issue:++1. Inspect declared ports and assigned pods.++    ```bash+    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml+    kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=<eligible-node> -o yaml+    ```+2. Release only an obsolete authorized reservation, choose a nonconflicting port, or provide another eligible node.+3. If the workload doesn't need direct host-port binding, use an appropriate Service design instead.+4. Confirm scheduling and the application's intended network behavior. Successful scheduling alone doesn't confirm that an application is listening.+ ## References  - [Kubernetes: Use Azure Disks with Azure Kubernetes Service](/en-us/azure/aks/azure-disks-dynamic-pv) - [Kubernetes: Use node taints](/en-us/azure/aks/use-node-taints) - [Kubernetes Documentation: Insufficient CPU](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/resource-bin-packing/#insufficient-resource)-- [Kubernetes Documentation: Assign and Schedule Pods with Taints and Tolerations](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/)+- [Managed AKS GPU node guidance](/en-us/azure/aks/aks-managed-gpu-nodes)+- [AKS GPU autoscaling example](/en-us/azure/aks/autoscale-gpu-workloads-with-keda)  **Third-party contact disclaimer**

This status code helps clients understand the purpose of the redirect. Application Gateway for Containers supports the following status codes in the `statusCode` field of the RequestRedirect filter: -- 301 (Moved permanently): Indicates that the target resource is assigned a new permanent URI. Any future references to this resource use one of the enclosed URIs. Use 301 status code for HTTP to HTTPS redirection.-- 302 (Found): Indicates that the target resource is temporarily under a different URI. Since the redirection can change on occasion, the client should continue to use the effective request URI for future requests.+| Status code | Meaning | Permanent | Preserves method and body |+| --- | --- | --- | --- |+| 301 | Moved Permanently | Yes | No. Clients may change POST to GET. |+| 302 | Found | No | No. Clients may change POST to GET. |+| 303 | See Other | No | No. The client follows up with GET (or HEAD) and drops the body. |+| 307 | Temporary Redirect | No | Yes. A client that automatically follows the redirect must preserve the method and body. |+| 308 | Permanent Redirect | Yes | Yes. A client that automatically follows the redirect must preserve the method and body. |++- **301 (Moved Permanently):** The target resource has a new permanent URI. Future references to this resource should use one of the enclosed URIs. Use 301 for HTTP to HTTPS redirection of browser traffic.+- **302 (Found):** The target resource is temporarily under a different URI. Since the redirection can change, the client should continue to use the effective request URI for future requests.+- **303 (See Other):** The target resource redirects the user agent to a different resource, as indicated by a URI in the `Location` header field.+- **307 (Temporary Redirect):** The resource is temporarily available at another URI. A client that automatically follows the redirect must preserve the request method and body. Future requests should continue using the original URI.+- **308 (Permanent Redirect):** The resource has a new permanent URI. A client that automatically follows the redirect must preserve the request method and body. Future requests should use the new URI.++Tip++Many clients rewrite a POST to a GET when they follow a 301 or 302 redirect, and the request body is dropped. If the redirected request isn't a GET or HEAD, use 307 or 308 instead. For example, use 308 rather than 301 for a permanent HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect when POST or other method/body-sensitive requests must retain their semantics.  ## Redirection capabilities

This article covers the security model, key features, and recommendations for validating security settings on Azure Linux.+Azure Linux 4 ships with Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) enforcing its targeted policy, and with SSH, kernel, and network hardening defaults applied. Azure network security groups (NSGs) filter inbound traffic by default; a host firewall is available when your workload needs one. -Note+These guides cover general-purpose Azure Linux 4 virtual machines (VMs). NSGs filter inbound traffic. IP forwarding, ICMP redirects, and source routing are disabled. | [Secure the host network](network-security) |+| Interactive access | On key-based deployments, SSH password authentication is disabled. Direct root sign-in is denied. SSH uses hardened session limits and SHA-2 message authentication codes. | [Manage identity and access](identity-and-access) |+| Guest disk encryption | The VM root isn't encrypted with Linux Unified Key Setup (LUKS). Guest-managed data-volume encryption requires configuration. Azure platform encryption is separate. | [Protect disks and data](disk-and-data-protection) |+| Cryptography | `DEFAULT` sets cryptographic defaults for applications that consume the system policy. Application overrides can change them. | [Use system cryptographic libraries](system-crypto) |+| Auditing and logs | `auditd` is enabled, but its default rule disables syscall and file-watch auditing. That coverage requires additional rules. The journal is persistent. | [Configure security logging and auditing](logging-and-auditing) |+| Packages | DNF verifies package signatures. Vendor files under `/usr/lib` and package-owned files can be replaced by updates. Provisioning options, extensions, and configuration management can change the results on your VM. -- **Hardened kernel**: With ASLR, stack canaries, and pointer restrictions.-- **Minimal package set**: Only essential packages for core operating system (OS) functionality. No legacy protocols, development tools, or non-essential daemons in the base image.-- **No external network connections by default**: firewalld denies all inbound traffic except SSH.-- **Key-only SSH authentication**: Password authentication is disabled.-- **Package integrity**: All packages and repository metadata are GPG-signed.+| Setting | Default | Set in | Check |+| --- | --- | --- | --- |+| SELinux mode and policy | `enforcing`, `targeted` | `/etc/selinux/config` | `sestatus` |+| Host firewall | Not installed. The `nftables` and `iptables-legacy` tools are installed, but no inbound filtering rules are loaded. | Not applicable | `rpm -q firewalld`, `sudo nft list ruleset`, and `sudo iptables -S` |+| Root SSH sign-in | `PermitRootLogin no` and `DenyUsers root` | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-permit-root-login.conf` and `30-azurelinux-cis.conf` | `sudo sshd -T`, then find `permitrootlogin` and `denyusers` |+| SSH password authentication | `PasswordAuthentication no` on key-based deployments | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf`, written at provisioning | `sudo sshd -T`, then find `passwordauthentication` |+| SSH session limits | `MaxAuthTries 4`, `LoginGraceTime 60`, `MaxStartups 10:30:60`, `ClientAliveInterval 180` | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/30-azurelinux-cis.conf` and `50-client-alive-interval.conf` | `sudo sshd -T` |+| SSH algorithms | System cryptographic policy, with message authentication codes limited to SHA-2 | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/40-azurelinux-crypto-policies.conf` and `30-azurelinux-cis.conf` | `sudo sshd -T`, then find `kexalgorithms`, `ciphers`, and `macs` |+| SSH pre-authentication banner | `/etc/issue.net` | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/30-azurelinux-cis.conf` | `cat /etc/issue.net` |+| `sudo` session handling | Commands run in a pseudo-terminal and are logged to `/var/log/sudo.log` | `/etc/sudoers.d/10-azurelinux-cis` | `sudo cat /etc/sudoers.d/10-azurelinux-cis` |+| Password hashing | `YESCRYPT` | `/etc/login.defs` | `grep ENCRYPT_METHOD /etc/login.defs` |+| Kernel parameters | Full address space layout randomization, restricted kernel pointers and log, restricted `ptrace`, unprivileged eBPF disabled | `/usr/lib/sysctl.d/70-azurelinux-hardening.conf` and the kernel build | `sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space kernel.kptr_restrict kernel.yama.ptrace_scope kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled` |+| Network parameters | Forwarding, redirects, source routing, and IPv6 router advertisements disabled; the default rule disables syscall auditing | `/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules` | `sudo auditctl -l` |+| Journal | Persistent | `/var/log/journal` | `journalctl --disk-usage` |+| Package signatures | `gpgcheck=1`, `repo_gpgcheck=0` | `/etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` | `grep -h gpgcheck /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` | -### Runtime protections+For CIS Benchmark and Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) status, see the [Azure Linux compliance overview](compliance-overview). -- **SELinux:** In Enforcing mode. Review both layers. For example, allowing a port in the guest doesn't override an NSG, and a managed identity grants access to Azure resources rather than an operating system sign-in. -- **SSSD/realmd**: Available from the Azure Linux repositories for hybrid identity scenarios with Active Directory and LDAP.+## Change security defaults deliberately -### Cryptography+Changes to security defaults require a documented workload requirement or approved baseline. Weaker settings can expose the workload; stricter settings can affect compatibility or performance. -- **FIPS 140-3**: Validated cryptographic modules with a simple enablement mechanism.-- **Post-quantum cryptography**: ML-KEM hybrid key exchange support.-- **System crypto libraries**: Applications can use OS-level crypto.--### Logging, auditing, and monitoring--- **auditd**: enabled by default; rule profiles ship under /usr/share/audit-rules/ and can be activated by copying the profile you need into /etc/audit/rules.d/.-- **journald**: Persistent storage with structured JSON output.--### Vulnerability scanning integrations--Azure Linux supports integration with common vulnerability scanning and security tooling. Note @@ -10,33 +10,35 @@ This scenario doesn't apply to Gen2 VMs on Linux node pools.  ## Prerequisites -- Azure CLI version 2.0.81 or later. See [Install Azure CLI](/en-us/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) for installation instructions.  ## Symptoms  Existing Windows Server node pools don't get upgraded from Gen1 to Gen2 when you [upgrade the node image](/en-us/azure/aks/node-image-upgrade) by using one of the following methods in Azure CLI: -- An entire cluster upgrade (by using the [`az aks upgrade`](/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az-aks-upgrade) command)-- A specific node pool upgrade (by using the [`az aks nodepool upgrade`](/en-us/cli/azure/aks/nodepool#az-aks-nodepool-upgrade) command)+- An entire cluster upgrade (by using the [`az aks upgrade`](/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az-aks-upgrade) command).+- A specific node pool upgrade (by using the [`az aks nodepool upgrade`](/en-us/cli/azure/aks/nodepool#az-aks-nodepool-upgrade) command).  ## Cause +The following causes explain why existing Windows Server node pools aren't upgraded to Gen2 VMs during a node image upgrade.+ ### Cause 1: Existing node pools aren't automatically upgraded to Gen2 VMs  By design, a node image upgrade doesn't support updating or upgrading existing node pools. The `az aks upgrade` and `az aks nodepool upgrade` commands upgrade only the node image (to a later node image version). These commands don't upgrade the corresponding VM generation. -### Cause 2: Cluster upgrade to Kubernetes version 1.25 or a later version upgrades only the OS+### Cause 2: Cluster upgrade to Kubernetes version 1.25 or later upgrades only the OS -When you upgrade your cluster to Kubernetes version 1.25 or a later version, only the operating system (OS) is upgraded (to Windows Server 2022). Existing node pools aren't affected. The associated Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets contain VMs that have the same Gen1 VM.+When you upgrade your cluster to Kubernetes version 1.25 or later, only the operating system (OS) upgrades to Windows Server 2022. Existing node pools aren't affected. The associated Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets contain VMs that use the same Gen1 VM.  ### Cause 3: Cluster upgraded and new node pool created by using Windows Server 2022 without specifying a valid VM size -After you upgrade the cluster to Kubernetes version 1.25 or a later version, you specify Windows Server 2022 as the OS to use on the node pool's VMs. However, the VMs don't use a Gen2 node image reference for one of the following reasons:+After you upgrade the cluster to Kubernetes version 1.25 or later, you specify Windows Server 2022 as the OS for the node pool's VMs. However, the VMs don't use a Gen2 node image reference for one of the following reasons:  - You don't specify a VM size, and the default VM size in the region doesn't support Gen2 VMs. - You specify a Gen1-only VM size. -When you upgrade the default OS from Windows Server 2019 (`Windows2019`) to Windows Server 2022 (`Windows2022`), the existing node pools aren't automatically upgraded to a different VM generation.+When you upgrade the default OS from Windows Server 2019 (`Windows2019`) to Windows Server 2022 (`Windows2022`), the existing node pools don't automatically upgrade to a different VM generation.  ## Solution

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            @@ -1,41 +1,88 @@ # Azure Linux Official Support Options | Microsoft Learn -Azure Linux provides official support for customers running workloads on Azure in supported scenarios. This includes support for virtual machines (VMs), virtual machine scale sets (VMSS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) container hosts, and Azure Linux container images.--This article outlines the official support options available for Azure Linux, including how to get production support, report bugs and documentation issues, report security vulnerabilities, and engage with the community through office hours and community calls.+This article outlines the official support options available for Azure Linux, including how to get support, report bugs and documentation issues, report security vulnerabilities, and engage with the community through office hours and community calls.  Important  Azure Linux is open source, but Microsoft support and lifecycle commitments apply only to **Azure scenarios**. Specifically: -- Azure Linux Virtual Machines (VM) / Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS), AKS container host, and container images are supported.-- Bare metal, ISO images, on-premises, and other clouds aren't supported.-- Customized images are supported only when built on top of a prebuilt Azure Linux image (for example, with [Image Customizer](customize-images)).
